<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar NLL values across most models (ranging from -20.76 to -19.80). This indicates that a standard progress curve with moderate concentrations and no initial product can be fit equally well by multiple mechanisms, including substrate inhibition (M7), substrate-induced deactivation (M16), catalyst dimerization (M2), and product-induced deactivation (M12).
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but it confirms that we need to perturb the system with specific initial conditions to break these degeneracies.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the top models (M7, M16, M2, M12, M13), we need an experiment that simultaneously probes product dependence, catalyst order, and substrate dependence. 
By setting a high initial product concentration ([P]0 = 0.5), we can directly test for product-induced deactivation (M12, M17) or product inhibition (M5). 
By increasing the initial catalyst concentration ([cat]0 = 0.15), we can test for second-order catalyst interactions like dimerization (M2) or bimolecular deactivation (M13), which will scale non-linearly compared to the first experiment.
By increasing the initial substrate concentration ([S]0 = 2.0), we can accelerate substrate-induced deactivation (M16, M11) or observe substrate inhibition (M7).

Contrastive predictions:
- M12 (P+cat=>inactive): The presence of 0.5 M initial product will cause rapid, almost immediate deactivation of the catalyst, leading to very little to no reaction progress.
- M7 (S+catS<=>catS2): The initial product will not cause deactivation. The reaction will proceed rapidly due to the higher [cat]0, though the initial rate may be slightly suppressed by substrate inhibition compared to standard Michaelis-Menten.
- M16 (S+catS=>inactive): The reaction will start but will plateau much earlier than expected due to the higher [S]0 accelerating the deactivation of the catalyst.
- M2 (2cat<=>cat2) / M13 (2cat=>inactive): The higher [cat]0 will increase the rate of dimerization or bimolecular deactivation, causing the initial rate or final conversion to be lower than what would be expected from a linear 3-fold increase in catalyst concentration from the first experiment.
</hypothesis>
